title: Helping without taking over
description: Good help leaves the other person more capable and more in charge than it found them.

body.heading: Ask what would help
paragraphs: The golden question of helping is embarrassingly direct: “What would actually help?” It prevents the classic error of delivering the help you would want, in the way you would want it, to a person whose situation you have only guessed at.
Accept the answer even when it is smaller or stranger than your plan. The person inside the problem is the world’s leading expert on it.

body.heading: Leave the steering wheel with them
paragraphs: Taking over feels efficient and is usually a slow theft: of practice, of confidence, of the right to make one’s own mistakes. Carry the bags, but let them choose the route. Draft the letter, but let them send it. Help that keeps the other person driving is slower and better.
This matters doubly with children, elderly parents, and anyone whose independence is already under negotiation with the world.

body.heading: Know when to step back
paragraphs: Help has a natural end, and overstaying it turns support into supervision. Step back at the agreed point, cheer the result, and be available rather than adjacent. The best helpers are easy to reach and easy to dismiss.
If stepping back is hard, that is information about you, not them — worth a kind thought of its own.

takeaway: Ask what would help, keep their hands on the wheel, and step back on time.
